interactions.label: Which of the following is a key characteristic of stochastic effects of ionising

params.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic of stochastic effects of ionising radiation?

answers.text: They occur only above a threshold dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A threshold dose is the hallmark of deterministic effects such as skin burns and cataracts. Stochastic effects follow the linear no-threshold model — any dose carries some non-zero risk.
Increasing severity with dose characterises deterministic effects. With stochastic effects, it is the probability of harm that rises, not the severity.

answers.text: Their probability increases with dose, but severity does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Stochastic effects such as carcinogenesis and hereditary mutations become more probable at higher doses, but a radiation-induced cancer is no less severe whether the causative dose was small or large.
Early onset is characteristic of deterministic effects. Stochastic effects are typically late, often manifesting decades after exposure — the basis for long-term dosimetric monitoring.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the two categories: stochastic effects are probabilistic with no threshold (cancer, hereditary effects), while deterministic effects are severity-graded above a threshold (burns, cataracts, sterility).
Well done. The 'random probability, no threshold' nature of stochastic effects underpins the linear no-threshold model and drives all radiation protection policy.

interactions.label: A thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) badge is heated in the laboratory and emits

params.question: A thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) badge is heated in the laboratory and emits light. What does the intensity of that light represent?

answers.text: The type of radiation the worker was exposed to

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TLD badges measure accumulated dose through energy stored in their crystal. They do not identify the type of radiation that caused the exposure.

answers.text: The cumulative radiation dose received since the badge was last read

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The TLD crystal stores energy proportional to radiation exposure. When heated, it releases this stored energy as light — the brighter the emission, the higher the cumulative dose since the last reading.

answers.text: The instantaneous dose rate at the moment of reading

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The TLD records total accumulated dose over the wearing period, not the dose rate at any single moment. It functions as a cumulative recorder, reviewed quarterly.

answers.text: The effective dose in Sieverts for the specific tissue where the badge was worn

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Converting absorbed dose to effective dose (Sievert) requires weighting factors for radiation type and tissue sensitivity. The TLD itself measures physical dose accumulation, not biological risk.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: Gray measures the physics (energy deposited), Sievert measures the risk (biological harm). The TLD crystal stores radiation energy and releases it as light when heated — brightness reflects cumulative dose.
Exactly. TLD badges are cumulative dose recorders — the crystal stores energy from radiation, then releases it as measurable light when heated.

interactions.label: Patients undergoing diagnostic imaging are subject to the same annual dose limit

params.question: Patients undergoing diagnostic imaging are subject to the same annual dose limit of 20 millisieverts that applies to occupationally exposed workers.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. There is no annual dose limit for patients' diagnostic exposures. Patient protection comes from justification (ensuring each study offers a net clinical benefit) and optimisation (keeping dose ALARA). The 20 mSv/year limit applies only to occupationally exposed workers.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Occupational dose limits (20 mSv/year averaged over 5 years) and public limits (1 mSv/year) do not apply to a patient's own diagnostic exposure. Patient protection relies entirely on the principles of justification and optimisation (ALARA), not a dose ceiling.

interactions.label: During fluoroscopy, a clinician doubles their distance from the X-ray source. Ac

params.question: During fluoroscopy, a clinician doubles their distance from the X-ray source. According to the inverse-square law, what happens to their radiation exposure?

answers.text: It is reduced to one half of the original exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Radiation intensity does not decrease linearly with distance. The inverse-square law dictates a much steeper drop-off than a simple halving.

answers.text: It is reduced to one quarter of the original exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The inverse-square law states that radiation intensity falls in proportion to the square of the distance. Doubling the distance reduces dose to 1/(2²) = one quarter — making stepping back one of the most powerful and cost-free protection measures.

answers.text: It is reduced to one eighth of the original exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This would imply an inverse-cube relationship. Radiation from a point source follows an inverse-square law: doubling distance gives one quarter, not one eighth.

answers.text: It remains unchanged because the lead apron absorbs the radiation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Distance and shielding are independent components of the ALARA triad. Increasing distance reduces dose regardless of whether a lead apron is also worn — all three measures must be applied together.

overallFeedback.feedback: The inverse-square law: intensity is proportional to 1/distance². Double the distance → one quarter the dose. Triple it → one ninth. This makes stepping back the cheapest, most powerful radiation protection available.
Well done. Distance is the most powerful of the three ALARA levers — doubling distance cuts dose to a quarter, and it costs nothing to step back.

interactions.label: A surgical registrar routinely wears a lead apron during fluoroscopy but does no

params.question: A surgical registrar routinely wears a lead apron during fluoroscopy but does not limit screening time or maintain distance from the beam. Which radiation protection principle is most directly violated?

answers.text: Justification, because the procedures are not clinically indicated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Justification applies to the decision to perform the imaging procedure. Here the procedures are clinically indicated — the issue is how the registrar protects themselves during the procedure.

answers.text: Dose limitation, because the annual occupational limit of 20 mSv will certainly be exceeded

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While dose may be higher than necessary, the core breach is of optimisation (ALARA). Dose limitation sets a regulatory ceiling; ALARA demands that exposure be minimised well below that ceiling using all available measures.

answers.text: Optimisation (ALARA), because shielding alone is insufficient without time and distance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ALARA requires all three practical measures — time, distance, and shielding — to be applied together. Relying on a lead apron while ignoring screening time and distance from the source is incomplete optimisation and the most common real-world ALARA failure.

answers.text: The linear no-threshold model, because any exposure without all protective measures is unacceptable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The linear no-threshold model is a scientific basis for understanding radiation risk, not a protection principle. The three principles are justification, optimisation (ALARA), and dose limitation. The registrar's practice specifically violates ALARA.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three radiation protection principles are justification, optimisation (ALARA), and dose limitation. The registrar's error is one of optimisation — relying on shielding (lead apron) while neglecting time and distance.
Exactly. ALARA is a daily habit: time, distance, and shielding together. A lead apron without the other two measures is the classic — and most common — protection failure.
